AIM To identify herbal products associated with HILI and describe the type of lesion associated with each product. METHODS Studies were retrieved using Medical Subject Headings Descriptors combined with Boolean operators. Searches were run on the electronic databases Scopus, Web of Science, MEDLINE, BIREME, LILACS, Cochrane Library for Systematic Reviews, SciELO, Embase, and Opengray.eu. Languages were restricted to English, Spanish, and Portuguese. There was no date of publication restrictions. The reference lists of the studies retrieved were searched manually. To access causality, the Maria and Victorino System of Causality Assessment in Drug Induced Liver Injury was used. Simple descriptive analysis were used to summarize the results. RESULTS The search strategy retrieved 5918 references. In the final analysis, 446 references were included, with a total of 936 cases reported. We found 79 types of herbs or herbal compounds related to HILI. He-Shou-Wu, Green tea extract, Herbalife, kava kava, Greater celandine, multiple herbs, germander, hydroxycut, skullcap, kratom, Gynura segetum, garcinia cambogia, ma huang, chaparral, senna, and aloe vera were the most common supplements with HILI reported. Most of these patients had complete clinical recovery (82.8%). However, liver transplantation was necessary for 6.6% of these cases. Also, chronic liver disease and death were observed in 1.5% and 10.4% of the cases, respectively. CONCLUSION HILI is normally associated with a good prognosis, once the implied product is withdrawn. Nevertheless, it is paramount to raise awareness in the medical and non-medical community of the risks of the indiscriminate use of herbal products. fetched_contents.text: Long-term safety and efficacy of a highly purified plant-based nutraceutical for improving clinical parameters of liver function in healthy participants: a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial Abstract Background Liver function is foundational to human health. While numerous herbal extracts have individually been shown to improve liver function, there are relatively few studies on combinations of herbal ingredients that may have synergistic effects. In addition, capsule fatigue is a common problem when aiming to incorporate multiple ingredients to support liver health. With these gaps in mind, the goal of this study was to evaluate the safety and efficacy of a highly purified plant-based nutraceutical containing organic herbal extracts of turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger on liver function parameters. Methods A randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial was conducted to evaluate the efficacy of this nutraceutical liquid formula. Healthy adults were randomized 1:1 to receive the nutraceutical product or placebo (both 60 mL) twice daily for 180 days. The primary endpoint was change in liver function tests (alanine aminotransferase [ALT], aspartate aminotransferase [AST], alanine phosphatase [ALP], gamma-glutamyl transferase [GGT]) from baseline to end of study. Safety was also evaluated. The primary endpoint was compared between study arms via analysis of covariance. Results In total, 130 participants enrolled in the trial; 65 were randomized to each group. Mean improvements in ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT were significantly greater with the nutraceutical product than placebo (p ≤ 0.001). No adverse events were reported. Discussion Supplementation with this liquid nutraceutical formula improved the liver enzyme profile of healthy individuals, suggesting that it may mitigate a trend toward higher liver enzyme levels over time in a convenient manner that fosters compliance. Introduction The liver has many functions that are important to human health, including detoxifying the blood, processing nutrients from food, regulating blood sugar levels and bile production, storing important vitamins, producing proteins involved in blood clotting, helping to maintain a healthy balance of cholesterol in the blood, and producing immune cells (1). Liver health is typically assessed by measuring serum liver enzymes such as alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST), as well as markers of cholestasis (alkaline phosphatase and gamma-glutamyl transferase) and other markers. The overall prevalence of elevated liver enzymes has been increasing and is estimated to be approximately 10% of the US population overall (2), with a markedly higher prevalence among certain subgroups (3–5). The prevalence of elevated liver enzymes among overweight and obese individuals, in particular, may be as high as 50%. Chronic liver disease is emerging as a public health priority in India, with the incidence of metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease ranging between 8 and 20% depending on the region and contributing to 10 to 15% of deaths due to chronic liver disease (6). In light of this increasing prevalence, maintenance of liver health has become an especially an important component of overall well-being. Healthy lifestyle choices, such as eating healthy foods, maintaining a healthy weight, incorporation of physical activity, and avoidance of smoking and alcohol are key to support and enhance liver health (7–11). In addition to these general lifestyle practices, dietary and herbal supplements have become increasingly popular as a means to support liver health. There are numerous herbal extracts that have demonstrated benefits for liver health. For example, turmeric (Curcuma longa) has been shown to promote healthy liver cell metabolism and to support tissues, including liver, from oxidative stress (12). Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) has been shown to help facilitate the metabolism of lipids and insulin (13, 14). Ginger (Zingiber officinale) has been found to support healthy liver function, and to have antioxidant properties (15–17). Milk thistle (Silybum marianum) has long been used to support the liver’s filtration process and to promote overall liver health (18). While each of these ingredients have individually been shown to have some benefit to liver health, to the authors’ knowledge, these have not been studied together in a multi-ingredient formulation. The authors speculate that, when combined, there may be synergy between turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger due to the unique mechanisms of activity in supporting liver health for these individual ingredients. Supplements are typically available in capsule form, which may pose an inconvenience, particularly when multiple capsules are needed, making it difficult to adhere to routine daily supplementation. Studies on medication adherence frequently report that polypharmacy, or the need to take multiple pills each day, and pill size/difficulty in swallowing negatively affect treatment adherence (19, 20). This “capsule fatigue” may also apply to adherence to herbal supplement regimens. Alternative delivery methods may help alleviate capsule fatigue. fetched_contents.text: Liver Function Tests: MedlinePlus Medical Test What are liver function tests? Liver function tests (also called a liver panel) use a sample of your blood to measure several substances made by your liver. The most common liver function tests measure: * Albumin, a protein made in the liver. * Total protein. This test measures the total amount of protein in your blood, which includes albumin and globulins. These proteins are mainly made in your liver. * ALP (alkaline phosphatase), ALT (alanine transaminase), AST (aspartate aminotransferase), and GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase). These are enzymes that are mainly made in your liver. Enzymes are proteins that speed up certain chemical reactions in your body. * Bilirubin, a waste product your body makes when it breaks down old red blood cells. Your liver removes most of the bilirubin from your body. * Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), an enzyme found in most of the tissues in your body, but some of the largest amounts are found in your liver. * Prothrombin time (PT), how long it takes your blood to clot. Prothrombin is a protein involved in blood clotting. It's made in your liver. Some of these tests can show how well your liver is working and others can show whether your liver may be damaged by liver disease or injury. But liver function tests alone usually can't diagnose specific diseases. So, if your results are abnormal, you'll usually need other tests to find the exact cause. Other names: liver panel, liver function panel, liver profile hepatic function panel, LFT What are they used for? Liver function tests are most often used to help: * Find out if liver disease or damage could be causing certain symptoms * Learn how serious liver disease is after it has been diagnosed * Monitor liver disease over time and/or find out how well treatment is working * Check for side effects of certain medicines that can affect the liver Why do I need liver function testing? Many liver function tests are included in a common blood test called a comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP). Your provider often orders a CMP as part of your routine checkup to screen for liver and other diseases. You may also need liver function tests if you have symptoms of liver disease or damage. These include: * Nausea and vomiting * Lack of appetite * Fatigue * Weakness * Jaundice, a condition that causes your skin and eyes to turn yellow * Swelling and/or pain in your abdomen (belly) * Swelling in your ankles and legs * Dark-colored urine (pee) and/or light-colored stool (poop) * Frequent itching Even if you don't have symptoms, you may need to be tested if you have a high risk for liver damage. Your risk may be high if you have: * A family history of liver disease * Alcohol use disorder (AUD) * Obesity * Diabetes * Been taking certain medicines that may cause liver damage * Hepatitis or have been exposed to hepatitis (swelling of the liver from infection or injury) If you already have liver disease, you may need to be tested to monitor your condition and/or to see how well your treatment is working. What happens during a liver function test? A health care professional will take a blood sample from a vein in your arm, using a small needle. After the needle is inserted, a small amount of blood will be collected into a test tube or vial. You may feel a little sting when the needle goes in or out. This usually takes less than five minutes. Will I need to do anything to prepare for the test? Your provider will tell you how to prepare for your test. You will probably need to fast (not eat or drink) for 10-12 hours before the test. Certain medicines can affect your test results, so be sure to tell your provider about everything you take. But don't stop taking any medicines unless your provider tells you to. Are there any risks to the test? There is very little risk to having a blood test. You may have slight pain or bruising at the spot where the needle was put in, but most symptoms go away quickly. What do the results mean? Understanding abnormal liver function test results is often complicated. So, it's best to ask your provider to explain what your results say about your health. If any of your liver function test results are abnormal, your provider will compare the results of all the substances that were measured. This is done to look for certain patterns of normal and abnormal results that suggest different types of liver conditions. In general, the results of your liver function tests can tell you if: * Your liver is inflamed, which means you have hepatitis. * You have hepatitis from drinking alcohol or other causes, such as infection. * Your liver isn't working well and how weak it has become. * You have a problem with your bile ducts. Bile is a digestive "juice" that your liver makes. Bile ducts are the tubes that carry bile through your liver and out of your liver. * Medicines are harming your liver and how serious the damage is. Abnormal results don't always mean you have a problem with your liver. Other conditions can cause high or low levels of certain substances that these tests measure. For example, high levels of ALP can be a sign of bone disease or liver disease. So, your provider will also consider your symptoms, medical history, risk for liver disease, and any medicines you take. If you have been ill recently, certain types of abnormal results may be temporary. In this case, your provider may repeat the tests later to see if your results return to normal. ## What the science says about 'herbal detox' and liver health

The science on herbal detoxes is clear in one important way: there is no credible evidence that herbs actually remove toxins from the liver in the way marketed. Instead, the available evidence suggests that herbal products can be harmful, and the popular idea that “natural” products are inherently safe is misleading.

### Whether herbs remove toxins from the liver
The strongest evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis on herb-induced liver injury (HILI). It found that herbal supplements are increasingly used, but they are not harmless and can cause liver injury, including fulminant liver failure requiring transplantation or death in some cases [N1-F1]. The review also identified 79 types of herbs related to HILI, with many cases involving complete clinical recovery once the product is stopped, but still a notable proportion of serious outcomes [N1-F1]. This directly contradicts the idea that herbs are simply “detox” remedies that safely flush out toxins.

A second source reinforces that “liver cleanses aren’t recommended because they’re not FDA regulated, lack clinical evidence and don’t reverse damage from overeating or alcohol” [N1-R3]. The same source also states that liver function is foundational to health and that numerous herbal extracts have individually been shown to improve liver function, but it explicitly warns that “liver cleanses” are not supported by evidence [N1-R3]. The clinical trial on a plant-based nutraceutical containing turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger showed improvements in liver enzyme levels in healthy participants, but only in the context of a study designed to evaluate safety and efficacy in healthy individuals [N1-F2]. That trial does not prove that herbs remove toxins in the sense of a detox cleanse; it shows that some herbal combinations may improve certain liver enzyme markers in healthy people.

### Which herbs are commonly promoted and what their mechanisms might be
Commonly promoted herbs for liver health include milk thistle, turmeric, dandelion, ginger, and others such as green tea extract, kava kava, and several more listed in the HILI review [N1-F1]. The clinical trial explicitly names turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger as ingredients in the nutraceutical tested [N1-F2]. The review also highlights that some herbs are promoted for hepatic homeostasis, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and other beneficial effects [N1-R4].

Mechanistically, the evidence points to multiple possible pathways:
- **Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects** are repeatedly mentioned [N1-R2][N1-F2].
- **Support for liver cell metabolism** and **hepatic filtration** are cited for milk thistle and turmeric [N1-F2].
- **Lipid metabolism and insulin facilitation** are attributed to dandelion [N1-F2].
- **Antioxidant properties** are attributed to ginger [N1-F2].
- The review on hepatic diseases notes that medicinal herbs may address hepatic homeostasis and efficacy in disease states [N1-R4].

But these are not proofs that herbs “detox” the liver in a broad sense. They are hypotheses or mechanisms that may support liver function in specific ways, such as reducing oxidative stress, improving enzyme markers, or modulating metabolism [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R4].

### Strength of evidence for health benefits versus hype
The evidence is uneven and should be interpreted carefully. The clinical trial on the nutraceutical showed statistically significant improvements in ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT in healthy participants, but it was in a healthy population, not in people with confirmed liver disease or toxicity [N1-F2]. That means it supports a possible benefit in healthy individuals, but it does not support the idea that herbs can “detox” the liver or reverse damage from overeating or alcohol [N1-R3].

The HILI review is the most alarming evidence for hype. It shows that many herbs are associated with liver injury and that the market for herbal products is large and growing [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that most patients use these products for general health improvement, health maintenance, and weight loss, which suggests that marketing often drives use rather than scientific consensus [N1-F1]. In addition, several consumer and health guidance sources warn that supplements can be toxic to the liver because they may be contaminated, contain unlisted medications, or cause direct hepatotoxicity [N2-R4].

Overall, the evidence for health benefits is real in some contexts, but the evidence for a “herbal detox” that removes toxins from the liver is very weak. The strongest conclusion is that herbs may support liver function or have some beneficial properties, but they do not reliably “detox” the liver in the way marketed, and the risks of harm are real [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-F2].

## When a patient should see a doctor before using herbal detox products

The evidence supports a cautious approach: if a patient is considering herbal detox products, they should first talk to a doctor, especially if they have any risk factors, symptoms, or a history of liver disease. The available evidence also makes clear that liver function tests and specialist consultations may be necessary before starting these products, and that clinicians should be informed about possible drug interactions.

### Red flags indicating a medical need for evaluation
The strongest red flags are:
- **Symptoms of possible liver damage**, such as fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain, or skin issues [N3-R3][N3-R5].
- **Risk factors for liver disease**, including alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, hepatitis, or a family history of liver disease [N4-F3].
- **Use of medications or supplements** that may affect the liver, because herbal products can interact with drugs [N5-R4].
- **A history of abnormal liver function tests or liver disease** [N4-F3].
- **Use of herbal products that are known to be associated with liver injury**, such as turmeric, milk thistle, green tea extract, kava kava, and others [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

A Mayo Clinic source explicitly states that “some dietary and herbal supplements can harm the liver” and that “more than 1,000 medicines and herbal products have been linked to liver damage” [N3-R2]. This means even a person without obvious symptoms may still need evaluation if they are using products with known risk.

### What tests or specialist consultations are appropriate
The evidence suggests that liver function tests are the most relevant starting point. MedlinePlus and Mayo Clinic explain that liver function tests (LFTs) use blood to measure substances made by the liver, including albumin, total protein, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin, and others [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. The NHS source adds that these tests help assess liver function and interpret abnormal results [N4-R3]. The guidelines on abnormal liver blood tests note that they are used to find the cause of symptoms, monitor liver disease, and assess treatment response [N4-R4].

If tests are abnormal, the evidence supports further evaluation by a specialist. The liver function test source says that abnormal results usually need other tests to find the exact cause [N4-F3]. It also notes that symptoms, medical history, risk factors, and medications should all be considered [N4-F3]. Because herbal products can interact with medications, consulting a clinician is important for safe use [N5-R4].

### How to discuss supplements safely with a clinician
The evidence strongly supports open communication with a clinician before starting any herbal product. The BSW Health source advises patients to “talk to your doctor before taking herbal detox supplements and follow dosing instructions closely” [N3-R1]. The FTC and FDA guidance also emphasize that claims about supplements must be truthful and substantiated, and that consumers should be able to interpret labels and understand what claims mean [N6-R2][N6-R5].

A safe discussion should include:
- Any symptoms the patient is experiencing.
- Any medications or supplements they are taking.
- Any history of liver disease or abnormal liver tests.
- Any specific herbs or formulas they are considering.
- Whether they want to use a product for a general health purpose or a specific condition.

The evidence also supports caution because herbal products can have interactions with cytochrome P450 enzymes, which can affect drug metabolism [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. This means that even if a patient feels fine, they may still need a doctor’s advice to avoid interactions or harm [N5-R1][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion: patients should not start herbal detox products without first seeing a doctor, especially if they have symptoms, risk factors, or are using medications [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F3][N5-R4].

## How to assess liver function and what abnormal results mean for detox claims

### Which lab tests are relevant and what they measure
The most relevant lab tests are liver function tests, also called liver panels. MedlinePlus, Mayo Clinic, and NHS sources all describe these tests as blood tests that measure substances made by the liver, including:
- **Albumin and total protein** [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].
- **ALT (alanine aminotransferase), AST (aspartate aminotransferase), ALP (alkaline phosphatase), and GGT (gamma-glutamyl transferase)** [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].
- **Bilirubin** [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3].
- **LDH (lactate dehydrogenase)** [N4-F3].
- **Prothrombin time (PT)** [N4-F3].

These tests are used to assess how well the liver is working, detect liver damage or disease, and monitor treatment response [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-F3]. They are also useful for checking side effects of medications that can affect the liver [N4-F3].

### How abnormal results affect the interpretation of detox claims
Abnormal results make detox claims much less credible. The evidence shows that liver function tests alone cannot diagnose specific diseases, so abnormal results usually require additional testing to find the exact cause [N4-F3]. This means a person with abnormal LFTs may not have a “detox” problem, but rather a more serious condition such as hepatitis, alcoholic liver disease, bile duct problems, or drug-induced liver injury [N4-F3].

The evidence also highlights that abnormal results do not always mean liver disease. For example, high ALP can be caused by bone disease rather than liver disease [N4-F3]. Because of this, abnormal results must be interpreted in the context of symptoms, medical history, risk factors, and current medications [N4-F3]. This is especially important because herbal products can cause liver injury and can also interact with medications [N1-F1][N5-R4].

### Next steps if liver function tests are abnormal
If liver function tests are abnormal, the next steps are:
1. **Repeat tests if needed**, because some abnormal results may be temporary [N4-F3].
2. **Compare all measured substances** to look for patterns that suggest different liver conditions [N4-F3].
3. **Consider other tests** to find the exact cause of the abnormal results [N4-F3].
4. **Refer to a specialist** if the cause is unclear or if the abnormal results are serious [N4-R4].
5. **Stop or adjust any questionable herbal products**, especially if the patient is using supplements known to be associated with liver injury [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

The evidence also supports a cautious interpretation of detox claims in the presence of abnormal results. Since herbal detox products are not FDA regulated and may cause liver injury, abnormal LFTs should make the patient and clinician question whether the product is safe or whether there is another underlying cause [N1-R3][N1-F1][N4-F3]. In short, abnormal liver function tests should not be taken as proof that a “detox” remedy is working; they should instead prompt further investigation and caution about herbal use [N4-F3][N5-R4].

## Practical advice for choosing a remedy, dose, and dose form

### How to interpret product labels and dosage claims
The evidence shows that product labels can be misleading and that consumers may misinterpret claims. FTC and FDA guidance emphasize that claims about health products must be truthful, substantiated, and compliant with placement and type-size requirements [N6-R2][N6-R5]. The evidence also notes that consumers are more likely to believe specific disease-related health benefits when labels include those claims [N6-R1].

This means that patients should be especially cautious about:
- **Vague or exaggerated claims** such as “detox,” “flush toxins,” or “cleanse your liver.”
- **Unsubstantiated health benefits** that are not supported by the evidence provided in the label.
- **Marketing language** that implies safety or efficacy without scientific proof [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

A practical interpretation is to treat marketing claims as promotional rather than scientific proof. The clinical trial on the nutraceutical showed improvements in liver enzyme levels in healthy participants, but it was still a study in healthy people and not a proof of “detox” action [N1-F2]. The HILI review also shows that many herbs are associated with liver injury, so the same label that claims benefit may also carry risk [N1-F1].

### What dose ranges are plausible and what are not
The evidence does not provide a single dose recommendation for all herbs, but it does give useful context for what is plausible. The clinical trial used a highly purified plant-based nutraceutical containing organic herbal extracts of turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger, and participants took 60 mL twice daily for 180 days [N1-F2]. That is a specific, structured dose, but it was in a healthy population and not in people with liver disease.

The HILI review lists many herbs associated with liver injury, including milk thistle, green tea extract, kava kava, and others, and it notes that the products were taken in various forms and doses [N1-F1]. This underscores that dose ranges can vary widely and that there is no universal safe or effective “detox” dose.

The safest interpretation is therefore:
- **Plausible doses** are those that are used in controlled studies or clearly stated on the label.
- **Unplausible doses** are those that are not supported by evidence, are extremely high, or are not clearly defined [N1-F1][N1-F2].

### Warnings about self-medicating with herbal detox products
The evidence is clear that self-medicating with herbal detox products is risky. A systematic review on HILI found that herbs can cause liver injury, with some cases requiring liver transplantation, chronic liver disease, or death [N1-F1]. Another source warns that supplements can be toxic to the liver because they may be contaminated or contain unlisted medications [N2-R4].

The evidence also supports that self-medicating is especially dangerous when:
- A person has symptoms of liver damage.
- A person has risk factors for liver disease.
- A person is using medications that may interact with herbs [N5-R1][N5-R4].
- A person is using products that are known to be associated with liver injury [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

In short, self-medicating with herbal detox products is not advisable because the science does not support the idea that they safely remove toxins from the liver, and the risk of harm is real [N1-F1][N1-R3][N2-R4]. The best practical advice is to consult a doctor before starting any herbal detox product, and then follow the doctor’s guidance on dose, form, and duration [N3-R1][N5-R4].

3. **Consider other tests** to find the exact cause of the abnormal results [N4-F3].
4. **Refer to a specialist** if the cause is unclear or if the abnormal results are serious [N4-R4].
5. **Stop or adjust any questionable herbal products**, especially if you are using supplements known to be associated with liver injury [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

### 7. How to choose a remedy, dose, and dose form
The evidence suggests that product labels can be misleading and that consumers may misinterpret claims [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. So you should be especially cautious about:
- **Vague or exaggerated claims** such as “detox,” “flush toxins,” or “cleanse your liver.”
- **Unsubstantiated health benefits** that are not supported by the evidence provided in the label.
- **Marketing language** that implies safety or efficacy without scientific proof [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

#### Dose ranges
The evidence does not provide a single “best” dose for all herbs, but it does give useful context:
- The clinical trial used a highly purified plant-based nutraceutical containing organic herbal extracts, and participants took 60 mL twice daily for 180 days [N1-F2].
- The HILI review notes that many herbs are associated with liver injury and that dose ranges can vary widely [N1-F1].

So:
- **Plausible doses** are those used in controlled studies or clearly stated on the label.
- **Unplausible doses** are those that are not supported by evidence, are extremely high, or are not clearly defined [N1-F1][N1-F2].

#### Warnings about self-medicating
Self-medicating with herbal detox products is risky. The HILI review shows that herbs can cause liver injury, with some cases requiring liver transplantation, chronic liver disease, or death [N1-F1]. Another source warns that supplements can be toxic to the liver because they may be contaminated or contain unlisted medications [N2-R4].

Self-medicating is especially dangerous if you:
- Have symptoms of liver damage.
- Have risk factors for liver disease.
- Are using medications that may interact with herbs [N5-R1][N5-R4].
- Are using products known to be associated with liver injury [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

### 8. How to discuss supplements safely with a clinician
The evidence strongly supports open communication with your clinician before starting any herbal product. The BSW Health source advises patients to “talk to your doctor before taking herbal detox supplements and follow dosing instructions closely” [N3-R1]. The FTC and FDA guidance also emphasize that claims about health products must be truthful, substantiated, and compliant with label requirements [N6-R2][N6-R5].

A safe discussion should include:
- Your symptoms.
- Any medications or supplements you are taking.
- Any history of liver disease or abnormal liver tests.
- Any specific herbs or formulas you are considering.
- Whether you want to use a product for a general health purpose or a specific condition.

The evidence also supports caution because herbal products can interact with cytochrome P450 enzymes, which can affect drug metabolism [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. This means even if you feel fine, you may still need a doctor’s advice to avoid interactions or harm [N5-R4].

### Final recommendation
If you read that an herbal detox can “flush out toxins from your liver and keep you healthy,” the best answer is:
- **No, there is no credible evidence that herbs actually do this.**
- **Yes, you should probably get checked first.**
- **Yes, talk to your doctor before starting any herbal detox product.**

If you do decide to try a supplement, choose it carefully, interpret the label critically, and follow your doctor’s guidance on dose, form, and duration [N1-R3][N1-F1][N3-R1][N5-R4].

In short: **the safest approach is to prioritize medical evaluation before relying on “herbal detox” claims** [N1-F1][N3-R1][N4-F3].

## What the science says about 'herbal detox' and liver health

The science on herbal detoxes is clear in one important way: there is no credible evidence that herbs actually remove toxins from the liver in the way marketed. Instead, the available evidence suggests that herbal products can be harmful, and the popular idea that “natural” products are inherently safe is misleading.

### Whether herbs remove toxins from the liver
The strongest evidence comes from a systematic review and meta-analysis on herb-induced liver injury (HILI). It found that herbal supplements are increasingly used, but they are not harmless and can cause liver injury, including fulminant liver failure requiring transplantation or death in some cases [N1-F1]. The review also identified 79 types of herbs related to HILI, with many cases involving complete clinical recovery once the product is stopped, but still a notable proportion of serious outcomes [N1-F1]. This directly contradicts the idea that herbs are simply “detox” remedies that safely flush out toxins.

A second source reinforces that “liver cleanses aren’t recommended because they’re not FDA regulated, lack clinical evidence and don’t reverse damage from overeating or alcohol” [N1-R3]. The same source also states that liver function is foundational to health and that numerous herbal extracts have individually been shown to improve liver function, but it explicitly warns that “liver cleanses” are not supported by evidence [N1-R3]. The clinical trial on a plant-based nutraceutical containing turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger showed improvements in liver enzyme levels in healthy participants, but only in the context of a study designed to evaluate safety and efficacy in healthy individuals [N1-F2]. That trial does not prove that herbs remove toxins in the sense of a detox cleanse; it shows that some herbal combinations may improve certain liver enzyme markers in healthy people.

### Which herbs are commonly promoted and what their mechanisms might be
Commonly promoted herbs for liver health include milk thistle, turmeric, dandelion, ginger, and others such as green tea extract, kava kava, and several more listed in the HILI review [N1-F1]. The clinical trial explicitly names turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger as ingredients in the nutraceutical tested [N1-F2]. The review also highlights that some herbs are promoted for hepatic homeostasis, antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and other beneficial effects [N1-R4].

Mechanistically, the evidence points to multiple possible pathways:
- **Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects** are repeatedly mentioned [N1-R2][N1-F2].
- **Support for liver cell metabolism** and **hepatic filtration** are cited for milk thistle and turmeric [N1-F2].
- **Lipid metabolism and insulin facilitation** are attributed to dandelion [N1-F2].
- **Antioxidant properties** are attributed to ginger [N1-F2].
- The review on hepatic diseases notes that medicinal herbs may address hepatic homeostasis and efficacy in disease states [N1-R4].

But these are not proofs that herbs “detox” the liver in a broad sense. They are hypotheses or mechanisms that may support liver function in specific ways, such as reducing oxidative stress, improving enzyme markers, or modulating metabolism [N1-F1][N1-F2][N1-R4].

### Strength of evidence for health benefits versus hype
The evidence is uneven and should be interpreted carefully. The clinical trial on the nutraceutical showed statistically significant improvements in ALT, AST, ALP, and GGT in healthy participants, but it was in a healthy population, not in people with confirmed liver disease or toxicity [N1-F2]. That means it supports a possible benefit in healthy individuals, but it does not support the idea that herbs can “detox” the liver or reverse damage from overeating or alcohol [N1-R3].

The HILI review is the most alarming evidence for hype. It shows that many herbs are associated with liver injury and that the market for herbal products is large and growing [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that most patients use these products for general health improvement, health maintenance, and weight loss, which suggests that marketing often drives use rather than scientific consensus [N1-F1]. In addition, several consumer and health guidance sources warn that supplements can be toxic to the liver because they may be contaminated, contain unlisted medications, or cause direct hepatotoxicity [N2-R4].

Overall, the evidence for health benefits is real in some contexts, but the evidence for a “herbal detox” that removes toxins from the liver is very weak. The strongest conclusion is that herbs may support liver function or have some beneficial properties, but they do not reliably “detox” the liver in the way marketed, and the risks of harm are real [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-F2].

### Red flags indicating a medical need for evaluation
The strongest red flags are:
- **Symptoms of possible liver damage**, such as fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain, or skin issues [N3-R3][N3-R5].
- **Risk factors for liver disease**, including alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, hepatitis, or a family history of liver disease [N4-F3].
- **Use of medications or supplements** that may affect the liver, because herbal products can interact with drugs [N5-R4].
- **A history of abnormal liver function tests or liver disease** [N4-F3].
- **Use of herbal products that are known to be associated with liver injury**, such as turmeric, milk thistle, green tea extract, kava kava, and others [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

A Mayo Clinic source explicitly states that “some dietary and herbal supplements can harm the liver” and that “more than 1,000 medicines and herbal products have been linked to liver damage” [N3-R2]. This means even a person without obvious symptoms may still need evaluation if they are using products with known risk.

### What tests or specialist consultations are appropriate
The evidence suggests that liver function tests are the most relevant starting point. MedlinePlus and Mayo Clinic explain that liver function tests (LFTs) use blood to measure substances made by the liver, including albumin, total protein, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin, and others [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. The NHS source adds that these tests help assess liver function and interpret abnormal results [N4-R3]. The guidelines on abnormal liver blood tests note that they are used to find the cause of symptoms, monitor liver disease, and assess treatment response [N4-R4].

If tests are abnormal, the evidence supports further evaluation by a specialist. The liver function test source says that abnormal results usually need other tests to find the exact cause [N4-F3]. It also notes that symptoms, medical history, risk factors, and medications should all be considered [N4-F3]. Because herbal products can interact with medications, consulting a clinician is important for safe use [N5-R4].

### How to discuss supplements safely with a clinician
The evidence strongly supports open communication with a clinician before starting any herbal product. The BSW Health source advises patients to “talk to your doctor before taking herbal detox supplements and follow dosing instructions closely” [N3-R1]. The FTC and FDA guidance also emphasize that claims about supplements must be truthful and substantiated, and that consumers should be able to interpret labels and understand what claims mean [N6-R2][N6-R5].

A safe discussion should include:
- Any symptoms the patient is experiencing.
- Any medications or supplements they are taking.
- Any history of liver disease or abnormal liver tests.
- Any specific herbs or formulas they are considering.
- Whether they want to use a product for a general health purpose or a specific condition.

The evidence also supports caution because herbal products can have interactions with cytochrome P450 enzymes, which can affect drug metabolism [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. This means that even if a patient feels fine, they may still need a doctor’s advice to avoid interactions or harm [N5-R1][N5-R4].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion: patients should not start herbal detox products without first seeing a doctor, especially if they have symptoms, risk factors, or are using medications [N3-R1][N3-R2][N4-F3][N5-R4].

The clinical trial specifically used turmeric, dandelion, milk thistle, and ginger [N1-F2].

The proposed mechanisms include:
- **Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects** [N1-R2][N1-F2].
- **Support for liver cell metabolism and hepatic filtration** [N1-F2].
- **Lipid metabolism and insulin facilitation** for dandelion [N1-F2].
- **Antioxidant properties** for ginger [N1-F2].
- Broader support for hepatic homeostasis in the review on medicinal herbs [N1-R4].

Again, these are plausible hypotheses or observed effects, but they do **not** prove that herbs can remove toxins in the sense of a detox cleanse [N1-F1][N1-R3].

### 3. Is the evidence for health benefits strong or hype?
The evidence is **mixed and uneven**. There is some real evidence that certain herbs may support liver function in healthy people or in controlled studies, but the evidence is often limited by:
- Studies in **healthy people**, not in people with confirmed liver disease or toxicity [N1-F2].
- A lack of strong, broad clinical evidence for “detox” claims [N1-R3].
- A large number of herbs associated with liver injury, which raises concerns about hype and overuse [N1-F1].
- Marketing claims that are not always substantiated, as consumers are more likely to believe specific disease-related health benefits when labels include them [N6-R1].

So the evidence for health benefits is **real in some contexts**, but the evidence for a “herbal detox” that reliably removes toxins is **very weak** [N1-F1][N1-R3][N1-F2].

### 4. Should you see a doctor before using herbal detox products?
Yes. The evidence supports a cautious approach: if you are considering herbal detox products, you should **talk to your doctor first** [N3-R1][N3-R2][N5-R4].

#### Red flags that suggest a medical need for evaluation
You should consider seeing a doctor if you have:
- **Symptoms of possible liver damage**, such as fatigue, jaundice, dark urine, abdominal pain, or skin issues [N3-R3][N3-R5].
- **Risk factors for liver disease**, including alcohol use disorder, obesity, diabetes, hepatitis, or a family history of liver disease [N4-F3].
- **A history of abnormal liver function tests or liver disease** [N4-F3].
- **Use of medications or supplements** that may affect the liver [N5-R4].
- **Use of herbs known to be associated with liver injury**, such as turmeric, milk thistle, green tea extract, kava kava, and others [N1-F1][N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

A Mayo Clinic source explicitly states that “some dietary and herbal supplements can harm the liver” and that “more than 1,000 medicines and herbal products have been linked to liver damage” [N3-R2]. That means even a person without obvious symptoms may still need evaluation if they are using products with known risk.

### 5. What lab tests are relevant, and what do they mean?
The most relevant tests are **liver function tests (LFTs)**. MedlinePlus, Mayo Clinic, and NHS sources all describe these tests as blood tests that measure substances made by the liver, including albumin, total protein, ALT, AST, ALP, GGT, bilirubin, LDH, and prothrombin time [N4-R1][N4-R2][N4-R5][N4-F3]. The NHS source also explains that these tests help assess liver function, interpret abnormal results, and monitor disease or treatment response [N4-R3].

Importantly, abnormal results do **not** by themselves prove a “detox” problem. Liver function tests alone cannot diagnose specific diseases, so abnormal results usually need other tests to find the exact cause [N4-F3]. They may also be caused by other conditions, such as bone disease, alcohol use, or medications [N4-F3].

### 6. What should you do if liver function tests are abnormal?
If your liver function tests are abnormal, the next steps are:
1. **Repeat tests if needed**, because some abnormal results may be temporary [N4-F3].
2. **Compare all measured substances** to look for patterns that suggest different liver conditions [N4-F3].
3. **Consider other tests** to find the exact cause of the abnormal results [N4-F3].
4. **Refer to a specialist** if the cause is unclear or if the abnormal results are serious [N4-R4].
5. **Stop or adjust any questionable herbal products**, especially if you are using supplements known to be associated with liver injury [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

### 7. How to choose a remedy, dose, and dose form
The evidence suggests that product labels can be misleading and that consumers may misinterpret claims [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5]. So you should be especially cautious about:
- **Vague or exaggerated claims** such as “detox,” “flush toxins,” or “cleanse your liver.”
- **Unsubstantiated health benefits** that are not supported by the evidence provided in the label.
- **Marketing language** that implies safety or efficacy without scientific proof [N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5].

#### Dose ranges
The evidence does not provide a single “best” dose for all herbs, but it does give useful context:
- The clinical trial used a highly purified plant-based nutraceutical containing organic herbal extracts, and participants took 60 mL twice daily for 180 days [N1-F2].
- The HILI review notes that many herbs are associated with liver injury and that dose ranges can vary widely [N1-F1].

So:
- **Plausible doses** are those used in controlled studies or clearly stated on the label.
- **Unplausible doses** are those that are not supported by evidence, are extremely high, or are not clearly defined [N1-F1][N1-F2].

#### Warnings about self-medicating
Self-medicating with herbal detox products is risky. The HILI review shows that herbs can cause liver injury, with some cases requiring liver transplantation, chronic liver disease, or death [N1-F1]. Another source warns that supplements can be toxic to the liver because they may be contaminated or contain unlisted medications [N2-R4].

Self-medicating is especially dangerous if you:
- Have symptoms of liver damage.
- Have risk factors for liver disease.
- Are using medications that may interact with herbs [N5-R1][N5-R4].
- Are using products known to be associated with liver injury [N1-F1][N2-R3][N2-R5].

### 8. How to discuss supplements safely with a clinician
The evidence strongly supports open communication with your clinician before starting any herbal product. The BSW Health source advises patients to “talk to your doctor before taking herbal detox supplements and follow dosing instructions closely” [N3-R1]. The FTC and FDA guidance also emphasize that claims about health products must be truthful, substantiated, and compliant with label requirements [N6-R2][N6-R5].

A safe discussion should include:
- Your symptoms.
- Any medications or supplements you are taking.
- Any history of liver disease or abnormal liver tests.
- Any specific herbs or formulas you are considering.
- Whether you want to use a product for a general health purpose or a specific condition.

The evidence also supports caution because herbal products can interact with cytochrome P450 enzymes, which can affect drug metabolism [N5-R1][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4]. This means even if you feel fine, you may still need a doctor’s advice to avoid interactions or harm [N5-R4].

### Final recommendation
If you read that an herbal detox can “flush out toxins from your liver and keep you healthy,” the best answer is:
- **No, there is no credible evidence that herbs actually do this.**
- **Yes, you should probably get checked first.**
- **Yes, talk to your doctor before starting any herbal detox product.**

If you do decide to try a supplement, choose it carefully, interpret the label critically, and follow your doctor’s guidance on dose, form, and duration [N1-R3][N1-F1][N3-R1][N5-R4].

In short: **the safest approach is to prioritize medical evaluation before relying on “herbal detox” claims** [N1-F1][N3-R1][N4-F3].
